newsitem.title: INDIA: India's state copper giant seeks costlier imports.
newsitem.headline: India's state copper giant seeks costlier imports.

text.p: State-owned Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL) has sought an increase in metal import duties to overcome a cash crunch, but analysts said on Sunday the company should instead import concentrates to help it turn around.
HCL officials said the company had urged the government to raise import duties on copper products to offset losses due to high production costs and a steep fall in London Metal Exchange (LME) prices.
The company has set a policy that links its prices with those on the London Metals Exchange.
Officials said HCL has asked the Mines Ministry to raise the import duty to 60 percent for copper cathodes and wire bars and 65 percent for wire rods from the current 30 percent.
India annually consumes about 200,000 tonnes of copper. HCL produces about 65,000 tonnes annually and the balance is imported. HCL reported profits of 750 million rupees in 1995/96 (April/March).
Officials said low copper content in ore and high power tariffs in India led to higher production costs compared with the rest of the world.
Analysts said with the depletion in the quality of HCl's ore it would be better for the company to rely on imported concentrates. Concentrates carry a 10 percent import duty.
"Copper deposits in India are very limited. It is better to import copper concentrates from Chile and Mexico and go for conversion into metal," said one analyst who did not want to be identified.
As part of economic reforms initiated in 1991, India in March 1992 deregulated metal imports, abolished price controls and cut the import duty on copper.
The import duty has been brought down to 30 percent from a high of 140 percent during the controlled regime.
Analysts said judging by this trend any duty rise appeared remote in the 1997/98 (April-March) general budget, due to be presented by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on February 28.
"Those days are over. I do not see any dramatic increase in duties," said one analyst.
"It seems out of question for the government to cut duties," said another analyst.

Copper prices crashed following the Sumitomo crisis last June when the giant Japanese trading house announced it had lost an estimated $1.8 billion from unauthorised copper trades over a 10-year period.
Prices of copper on the LME, where much of Sumitomo's copper business was done, tumbled to a two-year low of $1,745 per tonne, but picked up later.
The analyst said metal prices at the LME were now steady with copper being quoted around $2,380 per tonne.
"The downturn is through and for some time there may not be a bad patch," he said.
Last Monday HCL raised the price of copper wire bars by nine rupees to 117 rupees per kg and of wire rods by 14 rupees to 126 rupees per kg.
"The copper market is going to be firm," said Bombay Metals Exchange president Sharad Parikh.
However HCL officials said in a span of a few months the LME price had dropped by $600 per tonne compared with the corresponding period in the previous year.

"If the present LME price trend continues throughout the remaining part of the year 1996/97 (April-March) and during 1997/98, HCL is likely to suffer a loss of 1.1 billion rupees during 1996/97 and 980 million rupees during 1997/98," one official said.
